replying_to: Replying to Byte Pair Encoding for Efficient Time Series Forecasting
display_title: Official Review of Submission1598 by Reviewer juUU

summary.value: This paper introduces a pattern-centric tokenization framework for time series inspired by Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) in NLP. It compresses frequently occurring motifs within time series into a single adaptive-length token. This addresses the inefficiencies and lack of adaptability inherent in existing sample-based or patch-based tokenization methods. During the decoding phase, the authors propose a lightweight post-processing method called conditional decoding, which minimizes quantization error without increasing computational overhead. Zero-shot experiments conducted on foundational time series models (such as Chronos) demonstrate that this approach substantially enhances efficiency while maintaining or improving predictive performance.

strengths.value:
This paper introduces a novel tokenization paradigm for time series, shifting from fixed patching to adaptive pattern extraction. This represents a significant breakthrough over existing time series tokenization methods (sample-based or patch-based). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed tokenization method achieves an average efficiency improvement of 1990%. This compression is crucial for processing lengthy sequences and reducing computational overhead in large foundational models. 

The proposed conditional decoding approach further enhances performance without requiring gradient computation or increasing computational overhead during inference. 

The paper provides a detailed analysis of how quantization granularity and the lower bound on keyword frequency influence compression rates and generalization capabilities.

weaknesses.value:
The entire framework and experiments focus on univariate time series, yet many real-world tasks involve multivariate dependencies. It would be preferable for the paper to include some discussion or experimental validation in this regard.

The conditional decoding module relies only on first-order dependencies (conditioning on the previous token), which may be insufficient for sequences with long-term temporal structure. Exploring higher-order or context-aware decoding could better capture complex temporal patterns.

The dataset scope is somewhat limited to relatively stationary benchmarks (ETT, Weather, Electricity, Traffic). Adding more diverse datasets such as Solar and PEMS-BAY would better test the tokenizer’s robustness under non-stationary and spatially correlated settings.
The paper does not report variance or confidence intervals. Given the large reported gains, it remains unclear whether the improvements are consistent across random seeds. Reporting averaged results with standard deviations would make the claims more reliable.

questions.value:
The proposed framework is presented and evaluated on univariate series. How would the motif merging and vocabulary construction generalize to multivariate time series where inter-variable dependencies are critical?

The method is primarily validated empirically. While the efficiency gains are clear, the paper lacks a formal justification for why the hierarchical motif merging approach, adapted from BPE, fundamentally improves generalization or reduces reconstruction error compared to fixed-size patching.

rating.description: 6: marginally above the acceptance threshold. But would not mind if paper is rejected

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer juUU,

Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and for your valuable comments. We have already conducted new experiments addressing your suggestions and have revised our paper, highlighting the changes in blue. We are happy to answer your questions in the following.

**Q:** Multivariate time series \
**A:** We agree that multivariate time series are of practical interest. Byte-pair encoding on the variate axis would be challenging as datasets differ in variate number and ordering. Specifically, for foundation models in zero shot setting that will operate on unknown datasets. To apply our tokenization to multivariate time series we would follow current literature that patches variates individually (Woo et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 
 2024; Ekambaram et al., 2024). While, the design of the Chronos model does not make it compatible with multivariate forecasting, applying byte-pair encoding on the time-axis for every individual varite would be directly compatible with recent foundation models in the multivariate literature (Woo et al., 2024).
 
 
**Q:** Conditional decoding is based on the first-order Markov assumption \
**A:** In our experiments, conditional decoding based on the first-order Markov assumption already leads to large improvements in prediction quality while being very lightweight with only $M^2$ parameters. For our tokenizer with high compression, this is only 484 trainable parameters. \
You are right that for more complex dependencies, conditional decoding with higher-order Markov assumptions might be beneficial. This is an intriguing idea. However, higher orders would increase trainable parameters exponentially. This approach could be prone to overfitting, as for every character combination, the number of training examples would decrease exponentially. \
In sec. 5.6 and tab. 19, we analyze training dataset size for conditional decoding. Already for first-order Markov conditional decoding, larger training datasets benefit the extraction of robust conditional decoding distributions. This is why we chose the first-order Markov assumption, which results in lightweight and performant conditional decoding.


**Q:** Nonstationary datasets \
**A:** Thank you for pointing us to that. We now conducted new experiments including the Solar dataset (see tab. 2 and tab. 11). While Chronos models achieve a MSE of 1.27, our tokenizer substantially reduces MSE to 0.49 while accelerating the model 4.54x. This demonstrates the generalization of our motif-based tokenization to nonstationary datasets. \
In appendix C6, we conduct a targeted experiment that further demonstrates the generalization of our tokenizer to nonstationary data.

**Q:** Standard deviations of reported gains \
**A:** We agree that the standard deviation of reported gains would improve our paper. \
**Efficiency:** Regarding efficiency measures that are central to our work, we now report standard deviations of inference time (L795). In all experiments, we achieve runtime standard deviations <2%. \
**MSE:** Following current foundation model literature, we did not report standard deviations of MSE (Ansari et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 
 2024; Ekambaram et al., 2024). Training multiple foundation models with different seeds is very expensive. For our experiments, we already used over 14.000 H100 GPU hours. Nevertheless, we now started new training runs for foundation models with our tokenizer and Chronos baselines with 5 different seeds. As this is an additional 4500 H100 GPU hours, these experiments won't finish until the end of this rebuttal. 


**Q:** Formal advantages of motifs compared to fixed-size patching \
**A:** Throughout our paper, we empirically demonstrate improvements in efficiency, prediction quality, and generalization of motif-based tokenization. Further, motif-based tokenization has two formal advantages over patches. \
**Adaptiveness:** Fixed-length patches are rigid and can not adapt to patterns of varying length and complexity. By design, our motif-based tokenization captures diverse patterns of different lengths. We analyze this ability empirically in sec. 5.4. \
**Complexity:** The time series forecasting task substantially differs between patches and motif-based tokens. Predicting a patch in continuous space is a regression task. Generating a motif is a classification task within a discrete vocabulary. This discrete classification substantially decreases the complexity of the prediction task (L216). 

Thank you for suggesting these additional discussions and experiments. We believe they improve our work. We hope we could address all of your concerns.

display_title: Official Review of Submission1598 by Reviewer s7n2

summary.value: This paper addresses the computational efficiency challenges faced by Transformer models in time series forecasting by proposing an innovative pattern-centric word segmentation method. This method solves the problems of existing word segmentation strategies generating excessively long sequences, leading to high computational costs, and their inability to flexibly adapt to patterns of varying lengths and complexities in time series data.

strengths.value:
A. This paper is the first to systematically introduce the highly successful adaptive word segmentation concept (BPE) from NLP into the time series domain, proposing the concept of "pattern tokens." This provides a novel and elegant perspective for solving the problem of representing variable-length patterns in time series.

B. In addition to proposing a word segmentation framework, it also introduces the ingenious optimization technique of "conditional decoding." This technique is computationally lightweight, requires no retraining, yet effectively compensates for the information loss caused by discretization, significantly improving the practicality of the method.

weaknesses.value:
A. The paper emphasizes the efficiency improvements in the inference stage but doesn't discuss the computational cost of the word segmenter itself (i.e., the pattern vocabulary construction stage). While mentioning that it's "quite inexpensive," quantitative data on the time and memory required to build the vocabulary on large datasets is lacking.

B. Conditional decoding is based on the first-order Markov assumption. However, the authors don't mention that for complex sequences with long-term dependencies, higher-order dependencies might be ignored.

C. The vocabulary used in the paper is built on a large-scale hybrid dataset (Chronos) to pursue zero-shot generalization. Could this lead to learned patterns being too general and lacking capture of key features in certain domains?

D. The paper demonstrates a compression ratio of up to 128x. While conditional decoding can compensate for some quantization errors, could such extreme compression cause some subtle but crucial patterns (such as transient outliers or subtle morphological differences) to be lost during word segmentation, thus failing to be perceived by subsequent models? The paper lacks theoretical analysis or targeted experiments on the information loss boundary.

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer s7n2,

Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and for your valuable suggestions. We have conducted new experiments addressing your comments and have revised our paper, highlighting the changes in blue. We are happy to answer your questions below.

**Q:** A: Computational cost of the word segmenter \
**A:** Thank you for pointing us to this missing but essential detail. We have now added further discussion regarding the overhead of tokenization. \
**Training:** For training our tokenizer (pattern vocabulary construction stage), we utilize a single CPU core. Training on a large dataset with 100M time series samples only takes 3.8 hours and 1.2 GB of memory for our tokenizer with medium compression (see tab. 9 and L803-L805). \
**Inference:** During inference our tokenizer encodes time series. We now measure tokenization and detokenization overhead. This overhead is <0.5% in inference time of our fastest models and therefore negligible (L793-L795). We further suggest executing tokenization as pipelined preprocessing operations on the CPU to fully mitigate this minimal overhead (L799-L801).

**Q:** Conditional decoding is based on the first-order Markov assumption \
**A:** In our experiments, conditional decoding based on the first-order Markov assumption already leads to large improvements in prediction quality while being very lightweight with only $M^2$ parameters. For our tokenizer with high compression, this is only 484 trainable parameters. \
You are right that for more complex dependencies, conditional decoding with higher-order Markov assumptions might be beneficial. This is an intriguing idea. However, higher orders would increase trainable parameters exponentially. This approach could be prone to overfitting, as for every character combination, the number of training examples would decrease exponentially. \
In sec. 5.6 and tab. 19, we analyze training dataset size for conditional decoding. Already for first-order Markov conditional decoding, larger training datasets benefit the extraction of robust conditional decoding distributions. This is why we chose the first-order Markov assumption, which results in lightweight and performant conditional decoding.

**Q:** C: Patterns in the Chronos dataset are too general \
**A:** Throughout our paper, our motif-based tokenization outperforms other tokenization approaches on various domains. We demonstrate improvements in prediction quality and efficiency on 6 datasets in a zero-shot manner. This indicates that our tokenizer has learned universal patterns for multiple domains. We now visualize these patterns in appendix C9 on page 32 for enhanced interpretability. Additionally, we demonstrate the superior robustness of our tokenization to noise, nonstationary time series, and transients (see appendix C6). \
However, we agree that there might be specific datasets or domains where generalization of patterns is limited. This is a general limitation of foundation models and is not only attributed to our tokenizer. In this case, we suggest simply training a new tokenizer, building a vocabulary of domain-specific patterns. Computationally, this is very cheap as we discuss above.\
Note that even if patterns do not generalize to specific domains, our tokenization does not "overlook" features but falls back to single-sample tokenization as we analyze in L1518-L1520.

**Q:** D: Subtle but crucial patterns such as transient outliers \
**A:** Tokenization of transient outliers or extreme values is an interesting aspect. \
**Transients:** For this rebuttal, we conducted a new experiment in appendix C6 on page 29 to analyze the tokenization of outliers. Our targeted experiment demonstrates that models with our motif-based tokenization achieve better MSE compared to Chronos baseline models. We further demonstrate that transient outliers are not "overlooked" by our tokenization but are tokenized more fine-grained instead. By design, our method falls back to single-sample tokenization in case of unknown patterns. \
Please note that in contrast to patches, our high compressions of up to 128 are not enforced but adaptive based on the underlying pattern. Only if there is an appropriate pattern in our vocabulary, we compress a time series into a single token. We achieve such high compressions only for simple patterns such as constant values (see the noisy time series in fig. 13.o). We discuss this adaptivity of compression in sec. 5.4. \
**Information loss:** The only error introduced by our tokenizer is the quantization error. In sec. 3.1, we analytically calculate the upper bound of this error in L157-L160. This maximum information loss applies to all time series samples regardless of whether they are outliers or not.

Thank you for pointing us to these missing details and suggesting new intriguing experiments. These additional discussions improve our paper.
We hope we could resolve all your concerns.

display_title: Official Review of Submission1598 by Reviewer gYoz

summary.value: This paper proposes a pattern-centric, adaptive tokenization scheme for time series forecasting . The method quantizes time series samples into discrete symbols and then merges recurring, variable-length patterns (motifs) to build a vocabulary. Authors also introduce conditional decoding as a lightweight, post-hoc optimization to reduce discretization error. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing methods in forecasting performance and efficiency, while adaptively handling diverse temporal patterns.

strengths.value:
1. The paper presents the first pattern-centric time-series tokenization scheme. By drawing on Byte Pair Encoding from Natural Language Processing, it adaptively compresses repetitive patterns in time series into individual Tokens.

2. The proposed method exhibits excellent computational efficiency, with relatively low computational effort required.

weaknesses.value:
1. The experiments are highly insufficient: Table 2 only includes 5 datasets, with only one setting considered per dataset. Table 9 selects overly outdated models, lacking models from the past two years—for instance, PatchTST, which adopts a fixed patch-partition approach, is not included. Additionally, the experimental results in Table 3 lack persuasiveness; as the authors themselves note, comparisons across different model architectures and pre-training datasets fail to demonstrate that the proposed Motif-based tokenization method outperforms Patch-based tokenization methods.

2. The paper is excessively brief in certain sections, specifically the Introduction and Experiment chapters. In contrast, the Appendices are disproportionately lengthy, and key experimental results are scattered across different sections—this significantly hinders readability. For small models, there are already quite a few studies on unfixed patches, yet the authors do not seem to have mentioned this.

questions.value:
1. Line 73: "All these transformer architectures rely on two basic tokenization techniques: using every sample as a token or extracting fixed-length patches from a time series." In fact, there are already foundational models from related studies in recent literature.

2. Line 347: "Due to their fixed length, rigid patches are unable to capture these inter and intra series variations." Please explain this viewpoint more clearly and should include additional experiments on patch-based models to support this argument.

3. Line 363: The paragraph starting with "Compared to the MOMENT model..." cites many models, including PatchTST, but only provides verbal descriptions—yet I have not seen any experiments on the compression rates of these models.

Dear Reviewer gYoz,

Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and for your valuable suggestions. We have conducted new experiments addressing your comments and have revised our paper, highlighting the changes in blue. We are happy to answer your questions.

**Q:** W1: Table 2 too brief \
**A:** In tab. 2, we aim for two settings that are of high practical relevance: the best MSE and the fastest model. We now list full results in tab. 11 and believe this improves our paper. We also added Solar, now demonstrating efficiency and MSE improvements on 6 datasets in a zero-shot setting.

**Q:** W1: Table 9 does not include PatchTST \
**A:** Our primary goal is to explore our tokenization in zero shot setting for foundation models. Because Chronos is the only foundation model with single-sample tokenization, we also added dataset-specific models that use single-sample tokenization (L921-L922). \
For patches, we already compare with multiple foundation models (see next question). This is why we did not include dataset-specific models like PatchTST. 

**Q:** W1: Isolated comparison of motif-based tokenization and patches \
**A:** We agree that this is an important baseline. We have now implemented a patch-based version of Chronos, altering only the tokenization method. It uses the same backbone architecture, training strategy, and dataset (see L244-251). We now compare our motif-based tokenization to patches in an isolated and fair setting. Here, our tokenizer outperforms patch-based models in 5 sizes, with 2 different patch lengths, and on 4 out of 5 datasets, demonstrating the benefits of adaptive tokenization (L302-L309, tab 3).
We have rewritten this section to provide greater clarity, highlighting the importance of this finding.

**Q:** W2: Missing experimental information \
**A:** We have added additional information and explanation of our experiments in appendix B and sec. 4. We are happy to further include details if specific information is still missing.

**Q:** Q1: Related literature \
**A:** We are not aware of time series foundation models with adaptive tokenization. For example, WaveToken is a special case of single sample tokenization, achieving no efficiency gains (L82). If you have specific literature in mind, we would like to include it in our discussion of related work.

**Q:** Q2: Rigid patches and diverse temporal patterns \
**A:** We are sorry for this misunderstanding. We have rephrased our paper in sections 5.2 and 5.4 to add more clarity. \
**Section 5.2:** Here we compare the *MSE* of motif-based tokenization and patches. For this rebuttal, we conduct new experiments that allow for an isolated comparison, where our tokenization outperforms patches in forecasting quality (see above). \
**Section 5.4:** Here, we compare *compression* of patches and our tokenization. While patches employ fixed compression rates across time series and datasets, our tokenization adaptively compresses patterns based on their complexity, providing greater flexibility. This way, we achieve adaptive compressions for different datasets. We have clarified the motivation for this chapter in our updated paper.

**Q:** Q3: Compression rates of patch-based models \
**A:** Thank you for pointing us to this missing detail. We now list the compression rates of patch-based models on page 25 and L367 as a reference. 

Following your suggestions, we believe that these new experiments and revised sections enhance our paper. We hope we could resolve all of your concerns.

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel tokenization method for time series forecasting inspired by Byte Pair Encoding from natural language processing. The approach involves discretizing time series into symbols and then iteratively merging frequent adjacent patterns into a vocabulary of variable-length motifs, enabling adaptive compression based on pattern complexity. The authors also introduce conditional decoding, a post-hoc optimization technique that reduces quantization error by leveraging conditional distributions of continuous values. The paper claims significant improvements in forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency over existing methods like Chronos, MOMENT, and Moirai in zero-shot settings.

strengths.value:
The adaptation of BPE to time series tokenization is creative and directly tackles the inflexibility of existing methods.
The study covers multiple model sizes, tokenizer configurations, and datasets, providing a broad empirical analysis.
The examination of token embeddings reveals meaningful correlations with statistical properties, adding depth to the methodology.

weaknesses.value:
The outperformance of patch-based models is not isolated to tokenization, as differences in architecture and training data confound the results.
Compression ratios are used as a proxy for efficiency without reporting actual inference times or FLOPs, overlooking potential overheads from tokenization and detokenization.
The benefits of adaptive tokenization are not rigorously tested against a range of fixed-patch lengths, leaving open whether adaptivity is truly superior.
The paper lacks clear visualizations of what specific temporal patterns the motifs capture, reducing interpretability.

questions.value:
1. Can you provide a controlled comparison where your BPE tokenizer is evaluated against fixed-patch tokenizers within the same model architecture and training framework to isolate the effect of adaptivity?
2. How do actual inference times compare between your method and baselines on standardized hardware, accounting for full tokenization and detokenization costs?
3. Could you visualize the top-K most frequent motifs as continuous-time shapes to clarify what temporal patterns they represent?
4. What practical guidelines do you recommend for selecting key hyperparameters like the number of bins and minimum motif occurrence on new datasets?

Dear Reviewer 8kzc,

Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and for your valuable comments. We have conducted new experiments addressing your concerns and have revised our paper, highlighting the changes in blue. We are happy to answer your questions as follows.

**Q:** Controlled comparison of our BPE and fixed-patch tokenizers \
**A:** We agree that this is a relevant baseline! We have now implemented a patch-based version of Chronos, altering only the tokenization method. It uses the same backbone architecture, training strategy, and dataset (see L244-251). This allows us to compare our motif-based tokenization to patches in an isolated and fair setting. Here, our tokenizer outperforms patch-based models in 5 sizes, with 2 different patch lengths, and on 4 out of 5 datasets, demonstrating the benefits of adaptive tokenization (L302-L309, tab 3).
We have rewritten this section to provide greater clarity, highlighting the importance of this finding.

**Q:** Inference time and tokenization overhead \
**A:** You are right that inference time is the measure of most practical interest. For our main experiments in sec. 5.1 we already report inference time including tokenization and detokenization overhead. The efficiency gains in tab. 2 and fig. 3, 19 are based on inference time, which is measured on standardized hardware. We achieve standard deviations of inference time of < 2% for all measurements. \
We have independently measured tokenization and detokenization overhead. For our fastest models, overhead is < 0.5% in inference time and therefore negligible. We have added further discussion in L793-L801 and L369-L372. \
Additionally, for a model size and backbone independent evaluation, we reported compression values on the tokenizer level. 

**Q:** Visualize motifs \
**A:** Thank you for pointing us to this. We think this is a great addition to our paper. We have visualized 48 motifs in fig. 22 on page 32.

**Q:** Practical guidelines for selecting hyperparameters for new datasets \
**A:** In sec. 5.5, L397, we found that our tokenizer with the least quantization bins has the best performance on unseen datasets. This is why we would select a low number of quantization bins. In L412, we find a minimum token occurrence of p=4000 to be best. \
Training a new tokenizer only takes 2 to 4 hours on a single CPU core and is very cheap (tab. 9). For best performance, we generally recommend hyperparameter tuning (appendix C1).

Thank you for your feedback. Adding these new experiments and rephrasing some sections for clarity improved our work. We hope we could address all of your concerns.

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thorough and constructive feedback. We are pleased to see positive feedback regarding the **key contributions** of our work. Reviewers consistently highlighted:

- the **novelty & originality** of using recurring motifs as time series tokens [8kzc, gYoz, s7n2, juUU]
- the **flexibility & adaptiveness** of our byte pair tokenization over rigid patches [8kzc, gYoz, s7n2, juUU]
- the **simplicity, cleverness & effectiveness** of conditional decoding as post-hoc optimization to reduce the discretization error [s7n2, juUU]
- the **practical significance** of substantial computational savings while improving or preserving MSE  [gYoz, s7n2, juUU]
- the **breadth of our empirical analysis** including many in-depth insights about superior zero-shot generalization and explainable token embeddings  [8kzc, juUU]

We deeply appreciate the reviewers' thoughtful feedback. In the following, we list all the addressed concerns (including new experiments and changes to our manuscript):

- an **isolated & fair comparison** where motif-based tokenization outperforms patch-based models on 4 out of 5 datasets (sec. 5.2, tab. 3) [8kcz, gYoz]
- a clarification of **real-world efficiency gains** in inference time in our main experiments and a dedicated discussion on tokenization overhead which is non-relevant in practice (L793-801) [8kzc, s7n2]
- a rephrased comparison of **compression rates of rigid patches and flexible motifs** that adapt to diverse temporal patterns (sec. 5.4 with additional information on page 25) [gYoz]
- additional information on **minimal computational cost** to train our tokenizer on a single CPU core (L803-805) [s7n2]
- a analysis on **a new dataset (Solar)** where our motif-based tokenization substantially outperforms baseline models reducing MSE from 1.27 to 0.49 (tab. 2, tab. 11) [juUU]
- a demonstration of **superior robustness to transient outliers (unknown patterns)** of our tokenization method (appendix C6, page 29) [s7n2]
- a **visualization of our motif-vocsbulary** for enhanced interpretability (fig . 22, page 32) [8kzc]
- **standard deviations** for reported inference time (<2%, L795) and MSE (rebuttal juUU) [juUU]
- additional information on **experiments** (sec. 4, appendix B) and full experimental results (tab. 11) [gYoz]
- Resolution of remaining questions and minor issues [8kzc, s7n2, juUU] 

All points are addressed thoroughly in the individual reviewer responses, supported by new explanations, expanded discussions, and additional experiments. We submitted the revised manuscript with all changes marked in blue.

Overall, these clarifications and additions meaningfully strengthen the paper and further substantiate its contributions. We thank the reviewers again for their constructive engagement, which has significantly improved the quality of our work, and we hope that the improvements, combined with our numerous strengths, including the highlighted novelty of our concept and practical significance, make a compelling case for acceptance.
